title: Treatment and disposal of wastewater
summary: BOD and its kinetics carry the numerical questions, and the distinction between BOD and COD carries the conceptual ones — COD is always higher because it oxidises everything, so a high COD/BOD ratio warns that biological treatment will not work. The treatment stages should be held as a progression of removal efficiencies: primary 30 to 40 percent BOD, secondary to 85 to 95 percent. For Nepal, waste stabilisation ponds and the septic tank plus soak pit are the technologies that matter, and the commonest professional error is treating a septic tank as complete treatment.

sections.heading: Characteristics of wastewater
sections.body:
**Physical, chemical and biological characteristics**, each with its measurement:

| Category | Parameters |
|---|---|
| **Physical** | **Total solids**, suspended solids (settleable and non-settleable), dissolved solids, colour, odour, temperature, turbidity |
| **Chemical** | **BOD**, **COD**, **TOC**, pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, chlorides, sulphates, oils and grease, heavy metals |
| **Biological** | Coliforms, pathogens, viruses, helminth eggs |

**Typical domestic sewage:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **BOD₅** | **200 – 300 mg/l** |
| **COD** | **400 – 600 mg/l** |
| **Total suspended solids** | **200 – 350 mg/l** |
| Total solids | 700 – 1200 mg/l |
| Total nitrogen | 40 – 60 mg/l |
| Total phosphorus | 8 – 15 mg/l |
| pH | 6.5 – 8.0 |
| Chlorides | 30 – 100 mg/l |

**Solids classification** matters because different units remove different fractions:

> **Total solids = suspended + dissolved**
> **Suspended = settleable + non-settleable**
> **Each of those = volatile (organic) + fixed (inorganic)**

**Primary sedimentation removes the SETTLEABLE fraction only**, which is why its BOD removal is limited to 30–40%. The **volatile** fraction is the organic part, and the **volatile solids** measurement (loss on ignition at 550 °C) is how the organic content of a sludge is quantified.

**BOD and COD — the central distinction:**

| | **BOD** | **COD** |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | Oxygen used by **micro-organisms** to oxidise the **biodegradable** organic matter | Oxygen equivalent of **chemical** oxidation of **all** organic matter |
| Method | Incubation, **5 days at 20 °C** | Dichromate reflux, **3 hours** |
| Time | **5 days** | **3 hours** |
| Result | **Lower** | **Always HIGHER** |
| Use | Design of **biological** treatment; discharge standards | Rapid control; industrial wastes |

**COD is always higher than BOD** because it oxidises the non-biodegradable fraction as well as the biodegradable one. The **ratio is therefore diagnostic**:

| COD/BOD | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **1.5 – 2.5** | Readily **biodegradable** — domestic sewage; biological treatment is appropriate |
| 2.5 – 4 | Partly biodegradable |
| **> 4** | **Poorly biodegradable** — industrial waste; biological treatment will **not** work well |

That inference is worth more than the definitions: presented with a wastewater whose COD is ten times its BOD, the correct conclusion is that an activated sludge plant will fail on it and a **chemical or physico-chemical** process is needed instead.

**BOD kinetics** — first order:

> **BOD remaining: L_t = L₀ · 10^{−kt}**
> **BOD exerted: y = L₀ (1 − 10^{−kt})**

with **k ≈ 0.1 per day** at 20 °C (base 10), or K = 0.23/day to base e.

**Confusing 'remaining' with 'exerted' is the standard error** in these calculations. The **exerted** value is what a BOD test measures — the oxygen consumed so far; the **remaining** value is the oxygen demand still to come.

With k = 0.1: **the 5-day BOD is about 68% of the ultimate BOD**, which is the figure to carry. Hence **BOD_ultimate ≈ BOD₅ / 0.68 ≈ 1.47 × BOD₅**.

**Temperature correction:**

> **k_T = k_20 × 1.047^{(T − 20)}**

so the rate roughly **doubles for a 15 °C rise**. This matters in Nepal, where sewage temperature varies substantially between the Terai and the hills, and between summer and winter — a treatment plant that works in Biratnagar in June may underperform in Kathmandu in January.

**Why 5 days at 20 °C?** The 5 days was chosen historically because that is roughly the travel time of English rivers to the sea; 20 °C as a convenient standard temperature. The values are conventions, not physical constants — which is why the ultimate BOD, though harder to measure, is the more meaningful quantity.

sections.heading: Treatment stages and unit operations
sections.body:
**The progression of removal is the organising idea:**

| Stage | Units | BOD removal | Cumulative |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary** | **Screens, grit chamber**, skimming tank | **Negligible** | — |
| **Primary** | **Primary sedimentation** | **30 – 40%** (SS 50–70%) | 30 – 40% |
| **Secondary** | **Biological** — ASP, trickling filter, ponds, UASB | 80 – 90% of the remainder | **85 – 95%** |
| **Tertiary** | Filtration, disinfection, nutrient removal | — | 95%+ |
| Sludge treatment | Thickening, digestion, dewatering, disposal | — | — |

**Preliminary treatment** protects the plant rather than treating the sewage:

| Unit | Removes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Coarse and fine screens** | Rags, plastics, large solids | Would **clog pumps and pipes** |
| **Grit chamber** | **Sand, gravel, eggshells** — inorganic, dense | Would **abrade pumps** and **accumulate in digesters** |
| Skimming tank | Oil, grease, floating matter | Would interfere with biological treatment |

**The grit chamber's design is a neat piece of reasoning.** It must remove **dense inorganic grit** (specific gravity ~2.65) while **retaining the organic matter** in suspension for biological treatment. Since both may be similar in size, the discriminator must be **density**, and that is achieved by maintaining a **constant horizontal velocity of about 0.3 m/s**:

> Fast enough that **organic matter stays in suspension**
> Slow enough that **grit settles**

Maintaining that velocity despite varying flow requires a **proportional flow device** — a parshall flume or a proportional weir at the outlet — which is why grit chambers have a characteristic control section.

**Primary sedimentation** removes settleable solids by gravity. Design values:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Surface loading rate** | **30 – 45 m³/m²/day** |
| **Detention time** | **1.5 – 2.5 hours** |
| Depth | 2.5 – 3.5 m |
| Weir loading | ≤ 185 m³/m/day |

As in water treatment, **efficiency depends on surface area, not depth** — with the qualification that sewage solids are **flocculent (Type II settling)**, so they coalesce as they fall and depth does help somewhat.

**Secondary (biological) treatment** — the two families:

| Family | Mechanism | Processes |
|---|---|---|
| **Suspended growth** | Micro-organisms **suspended in the liquid** as a floc | **Activated sludge**, oxidation ditch, SBR, **aerated lagoon**, waste stabilisation ponds |
| **Attached growth (fixed film)** | Micro-organisms grow as a **film on a medium** | **Trickling filter**, rotating biological contactor, biotower, **UASB** (anaerobic, granular) |

**Activated sludge process (ASP).** Sewage is aerated with a **returned population of micro-organisms**, which oxidise the organic matter and are then settled out in a secondary clarifier and **recycled**.

Key parameters — and the first is the master control:

| Parameter | Typical | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **F/M ratio** (food to micro-organism) | **0.2 – 0.4** | The loading on the biomass; controls everything else |
| **MLSS** (mixed liquor suspended solids) | **2000 – 4000 mg/l** | The biomass concentration |
| **SRT / sludge age** | **5 – 15 days** | How long the biomass stays in the system |
| **HRT** (hydraulic retention time) | 4 – 8 hours | How long the liquid stays |
| **SVI** (sludge volume index) | **50 – 150 ml/g** | Settleability of the sludge |
| Return sludge ratio | 0.25 – 0.5 | — |

**Sludge bulking is the classic ASP operating problem**: filamentous organisms proliferate, the sludge will not settle (**SVI above about 150**), and it washes out of the clarifier — so the plant loses its biomass and its treatment simultaneously. Causes include **low F/M, low DO, nutrient deficiency and low pH**; the responses are chlorination of the return sludge, adjusting F/M, and correcting the underlying condition.

That the **sludge age (SRT) is separately controllable from the hydraulic retention time** is what makes ASP powerful: by recycling the biomass, the organisms are retained for days while the water passes through in hours. That decoupling is the whole idea of "activated" sludge.

**Trickling filter.** Sewage is distributed over a bed of stone or plastic media on which a **biological film** grows; air passes through the voids.

| Type | Loading | Recirculation |
|---|---|---|
| **Low rate (standard)** | 1 – 4 m³/m²/day | None |
| **High rate** | 10 – 40 m³/m²/day | **Yes** |

**Sloughing** is the periodic detachment of excess film, which must then be removed in a secondary clarifier — the trickling filter's own sludge production. Its advantages over ASP are **simplicity, lower power, and tolerance of shock loads**; its disadvantages are **lower efficiency, filter flies and odour**, and a larger footprint.

**UASB (upflow anaerobic sludge blanket)** deserves attention as the process most suited to warm climates: sewage flows **upward** through a blanket of **granular anaerobic sludge**, which degrades the organics **without aeration** and produces **biogas**. Its merits are **no aeration energy** (the largest running cost of ASP), **low sludge production**, and **energy recovery** — but it needs a **warm** temperature (above about 20 °C), gives only **65–75% BOD removal**, and requires **post-treatment** before discharge. It is widely used in India and is appropriate for Nepal's Terai.

sections.heading: Low-cost treatment and on-site sanitation
sections.body:
**Waste stabilisation ponds are the most appropriate technology for small Nepali towns**, and the reasons are worth stating clearly:

| Advantage | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **No mechanical parts** | Nothing to break, no spares to import |
| **No power** | Works where the supply is unreliable or absent |
| **Minimal operator skill** | The commonest reason plants fail is lack of trained staff |
| **Very low running cost** | Sustainable on a municipal budget |
| **Excellent pathogen removal** | Better than ASP, through sunlight and long detention |
| Tolerant of shock loads | Large volume buffers variation |

Against which: it needs **a large land area** (the decisive constraint in a valley town) and gives less control over the effluent quality.

**The pond series:**

| Pond | Depth | Detention | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Anaerobic** | **2.5 – 5 m** | 1 – 5 days | **Settles solids and digests them anaerobically**; high BOD removal per unit area |
| **Facultative** | **1 – 2 m** | 5 – 30 days | **Aerobic at the top** (algae supply oxygen), **anaerobic at the bottom** |
| **Maturation** | **1 – 1.5 m** | 5 – 20 days each | **Pathogen removal** by sunlight, pH rise and long detention |

**The facultative pond is the characteristic unit**, and its two-layer behaviour is the examinable point: **algae** in the upper layer photosynthesise, producing **oxygen** which the bacteria use to oxidise the organic matter, while the bacteria produce the **CO₂** the algae need. It is a self-sustaining symbiosis requiring no external input but **sunlight** — which is why the pond is shallow and why performance falls in cloudy weather.

**Maturation ponds achieve pathogen removal that no conventional plant matches**, through **ultraviolet in sunlight**, the **high pH** generated by algal photosynthesis, and simple **long detention**. Faecal coliform removal of **99.99%** over a pond series is achievable, which makes the effluent suitable for restricted irrigation.

**Other low-cost options:**

| Process | Character |
|---|---|
| **Aerated lagoon** | A pond with mechanical aeration — smaller area than a facultative pond, but needs power |
| **Oxidation ditch** | A continuous loop channel with brush aerators; simple ASP variant, tolerant and reliable |
| **Constructed wetland (reed bed)** | Flow through gravel planted with reeds; excellent polishing, low cost, attractive |
| Duckweed / algal pond | Nutrient recovery, fish or fodder production |
| **Septic tank + soak pit** | On-site, for individual buildings |
| **DEWATS** | Decentralised systems combining settler, anaerobic baffled reactor, filter and wetland |

**Constructed wetlands have been adopted successfully in Nepal**, notably for institutional and hospital wastewater, because they need no power, look like a garden, and can be maintained by unskilled staff.

**Septic tank and soak pit** — and the most consequential misunderstanding in the whole subchapter:

> **A septic tank is NOT complete treatment.** It provides only **settling and anaerobic digestion**, removing about **30 – 50% of BOD** and most suspended solids. Its **effluent is still grossly polluted and must NOT be discharged to a watercourse or drain.**

It requires a **soak pit, dispersion trench or drain field** to complete the treatment by **percolation through the soil**, where the remaining organic matter is oxidised biologically.

Design requirements (**IS 2470**):

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Detention time** | **1 – 3 days** at daily sewage flow |
| **Compartments** | **At least two** — the first settles, the second polishes |
| **Desludging** | Every **2 – 3 years** |
| Minimum width | 750 mm |
| Minimum depth | 1 m below water level, plus 300 mm free board |
| **Inlet and outlet** | **Baffled or T-pipes**, to prevent scum and sludge escaping |
| Ventilation | Pipe above roof level |

**Why two compartments:** the first receives the incoming disturbance and does the bulk of the settling; the second is quiescent and catches solids carried over. A single-compartment tank passes far more solids to the soak pit and clogs it.

**The soak pit** must be sized from the **percolation capacity of the soil**, determined by a **percolation test**. It fails where the soil is **clayey** (too slow) or where the **water table is high** (no unsaturated soil to treat the effluent, and a direct route to groundwater). In such conditions an **elevated dispersion trench**, a **mound system** or a small **package plant** is needed instead.

**Faecal sludge management** is the neglected half of on-site sanitation and increasingly examined. A septic tank desludged every two or three years produces **faecal sludge** that must be **collected, transported and treated** — and in most Nepali towns it is emptied by tanker and dumped, untreated, in a river or field. **Faecal sludge treatment plants** using **drying beds, co-composting or co-treatment** are the missing infrastructure, and building toilets without them simply moves the problem.

**Sludge treatment** for a conventional plant:

> **Thickening → Digestion (stabilisation) → Conditioning → Dewatering → Disposal or reuse**

**Anaerobic digestion** proceeds in four steps: **hydrolysis → acidogenesis → acetogenesis → methanogenesis**. It reduces volume, destroys pathogens, and produces **biogas of 60–70% methane** — a genuine energy recovery. Optimum conditions: **mesophilic 30–38 °C** or **thermophilic 50–57 °C**, **pH 6.8–7.2**, and 15–30 days detention.

**Methanogens are the slowest and most sensitive step**, so a shock load of acid or a pH drop **stalls the digester**: the acid-forming bacteria continue while the methane formers are inhibited, acid accumulates, and the pH falls further. Recovery requires reducing the loading and adding alkalinity — and the lesson is that a digester is controlled by **monitoring pH and volatile acids**, not merely gas production.

**Dewatering:** **drying beds** (simplest, needs land and sun — ideal for Nepal), **centrifuge**, **belt press**, **filter press**, **vacuum filter**. **Disposal or reuse:** **agricultural application** (valuable, subject to pathogen and heavy metal limits), **composting**, landfill, incineration.

sections.heading: Disposal, self-purification and standards
sections.body:
**Methods of disposal:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Dilution into a watercourse** | The commonest; relies on the river's **self-purification** capacity |
| **Land treatment / irrigation** | Uses the effluent's **water and nutrients**; needs land and pathogen control |
| Sea outfall | Coastal cities; not applicable to Nepal |
| Deep well injection | Special cases |
| **Reuse** | Irrigation, industrial cooling, toilet flushing, groundwater recharge |

**Self-purification of a stream** is the natural process on which dilution depends, and it operates through **dilution, sedimentation, oxidation (by dissolved oxygen), sunlight and time**.

**The Streeter–Phelps oxygen sag curve** describes it quantitatively. Two competing processes act:

| Process | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Deoxygenation** by BOD exertion | **Consumes** DO |
| **Reaeration** from the atmosphere | **Restores** DO |

> **D_t = [k_d L₀/(k_r − k_d)](10^{−k_d t} − 10^{−k_r t}) + D₀ · 10^{−k_r t}**

The DO falls to a minimum at the **critical point** and then recovers. The critical deficit is what matters, because if it exceeds the available DO the river goes **anaerobic** — fish die, the water turns black and smells of H₂S, and recovery takes far longer.

**Factors improving self-purification:**

| Factor | Why |
|---|---|
| **High turbulence and velocity** | Increases **reaeration** |
| **Low temperature** | Higher DO **saturation** and slower BOD exertion |
| **Large dilution** | Lower initial BOD concentration |
| **Sunlight** | Algal photosynthesis adds oxygen; UV kills pathogens |
| Shallow depth | More surface area per volume for reaeration |

**A fast, cold, turbulent Himalayan river therefore self-purifies far better than a sluggish warm one** — which is a genuine advantage for Nepal's hill rivers and a false comfort for its valley rivers in the dry season, when flow is minimal and dilution nearly absent. The **Bagmati** in Kathmandu is the standing example: in monsoon it dilutes and recovers, in the dry season it is effectively an open sewer.

**The dry season is therefore the design case** for any discharge, since dilution is least and temperature is often highest. Designing a discharge on annual average flow is a serious error.

**Effluent standards** vary with the receiving environment, and the logic is consistent — the more sensitive the destination, the stricter the limit:

| Discharged to | BOD limit (typical) |
|---|---|
| **Inland surface water** | **30 mg/l** |
| **Public sewer** | **350 mg/l** (the treatment plant will handle it) |
| **Land for irrigation** | **100 mg/l** |
| Marine coastal | 100 mg/l |

Nepal's **Generic Standards (2058/2001)** and the industry-specific **Tolerance Limits** set the applicable values, administered under the **Environment Protection Act 2076 (2019)**.

Note the **public sewer** limit is much more lenient, because the effluent will be treated downstream — the standard exists only to protect the sewer and the plant from damage (corrosion, toxicity to the biomass, blockage), not to protect a watercourse.

**Eutrophication** is the nutrient-driven problem that BOD standards alone do not address:

> **Nutrient enrichment (N and P) → algal bloom → algae die → decomposition consumes DO → fish kill**

**Phosphorus is usually the limiting nutrient in fresh water**, so its removal gives the greatest benefit per rupee spent — which is why phosphate removal, not nitrogen removal, is the first tertiary step for a lake or reservoir discharge. Removal is by **chemical precipitation** (alum, lime, ferric) or **biological (enhanced) phosphorus removal**.

**Nitrogen removal** requires two sequential biological steps, and both must be provided:

> **Nitrification** (aerobic): NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻, by **Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter**
> **Denitrification** (anoxic): NO₃⁻ → N₂ gas, needing a **carbon source**

The pairing is the point: nitrification alone converts ammonia to nitrate, which is still a nutrient and a health concern; only **denitrification** actually removes nitrogen from the water, as gas. And it must occur under **anoxic** conditions with organic carbon available — which is why nitrogen-removing plants have deliberately unaerated zones.

**Wastewater reuse** deserves the closing note, because it is the direction practice is moving. Treated effluent is a **resource**, not merely a liability: it carries water and nutrients, and in a water-scarce setting its reuse for **irrigation, industrial cooling, toilet flushing and groundwater recharge** displaces fresh water abstraction. The constraints are **pathogen control** (WHO guidelines set the standards for restricted and unrestricted irrigation), **heavy metals and salinity** where industrial waste is present, and **public acceptance**. The safest and commonest application is **restricted irrigation** of non-food or processed crops, which is exactly what a well-designed pond series produces.

formulas.label: BOD kinetics
formulas.expression: remaining L_t = L₀ 10^{−kt} ;   exerted y = L₀(1 − 10^{−kt}) ;   k ≈ 0.1/day at 20 °C
formulas.note: BOD₅ ≈ 68% of ultimate. Do not confuse 'remaining' with 'exerted' — the test measures exerted.

formulas.label: Temperature correction
formulas.note: The rate roughly doubles for a 15 °C rise — significant between the Terai and the hills.

formulas.label: COD/BOD ratio
formulas.note: COD is ALWAYS higher. A high ratio warns that biological treatment will not work.

formulas.label: Removal efficiencies
formulas.expression: primary 30–40% BOD (50–70% SS) ;   secondary to 85–95% overall
formulas.note: Preliminary treatment removes essentially no BOD — it protects the plant.

formulas.label: Grit chamber velocity
formulas.note: Fast enough to keep organics suspended, slow enough to settle grit — needs a proportional flow control.

formulas.label: Activated sludge parameters
formulas.expression: F/M 0.2–0.4 ;  MLSS 2000–4000 mg/l ;  SRT 5–15 days ;  HRT 4–8 h ;  SVI 50–150 ml/g
formulas.note: SVI above ~150 indicates bulking sludge — the classic ASP operating failure.

formulas.label: Waste stabilisation pond series
formulas.expression: anaerobic (2.5–5 m, 1–5 d) → facultative (1–2 m, 5–30 d) → maturation (1–1.5 m, 5–20 d each)
formulas.note: The facultative pond works by algal–bacterial symbiosis; maturation ponds give 99.99% pathogen removal.

formulas.label: Septic tank
formulas.expression: detention 1–3 days, at least two compartments, desludge every 2–3 years — removes only 30–50% BOD
formulas.note: NOT complete treatment. The effluent REQUIRES a soak pit or drain field.

formulas.label: Streeter–Phelps oxygen sag
formulas.note: The DRY SEASON is the design case — least dilution, often highest temperature.

formulas.label: Nitrogen removal
formulas.expression: Nitrification (aerobic): NH₄⁺ → NO₃⁻.   Denitrification (anoxic, needs carbon): NO₃⁻ → N₂.
formulas.note: Only denitrification actually REMOVES nitrogen. Phosphorus is usually the limiting nutrient in fresh water.
